abstract: Discharge of fruit fly sleep-promoting neurons is coupled to mitochondrial activity1. In vertebrates, adenosine accumulation resulting from adenosine triphosphate metabolization triggers sleep2. Such observations and theoretical considerations3,4 prompted us to investigate the link between neural mitochondria and sleep duration. To this end, we measured mitochondrial cross-sections in electron microscopy micrographs from publications of nerve or brain mitochondria in 51 mammalian species. There was considerable within-species variability of mitochondrial cross-section areas and we only included species where measurements from at least two publications could be made. Across 50 of the 51 species the average neural mitochondrial cross-section area decreased roughly exponentially with sleep duration (r = -0.76, p < 0.0001). The naked mole rat was an outlier having large brain mitochondria and long sleep. We also observed a significant decrease of sleep duration with body weight, and a multiple linear regression using sleep duration and body weight explained about 64% of the variance of mitochondrial cross-section areas. We suggest that the urge to sleep might be biophysically linked to mitochondrial size and mitochondrial leakage. Specifically, size-related decreases of mitochondrial surface-to-volume-ratio might reduce the need for sleep by decreasing mitochondrial leakage of reactive oxygen species (ROS). We identify neural mitochondrial size as a possible cellular determinant of sleep duration.
